analysisMarkdown:
## Where gold sits today

Spot gold is **$3,642.66** per ounce, up **2.26%** on the day. That daily gain is a bounce, not a trend change: the price is **33.7% below** its 52-week high of $5,496 set on 2026-01-29, and it sits just above the 52-week low of $3,533 printed on 2026-11-21. Gold trades **7.9% below** its 50-day average ($3,955) and **13.4% below** its 200-day average ($4,206). Trailing returns are negative across the board: **-10.2%** over 20 days, **-18.4%** over 90 days and **-12.5%** over the past year. Annualised 20-day volatility of **30%** underlines how choppy the tape has been, with the 20-day closing range stretching from $3,533 to $4,121.

## The macro backdrop

The macro picture is the core of the story. The **broad dollar index** stands at 123.60, higher than **100%** of readings in the past year, and it has strengthened **1.86%** over 30 days and **4.69%** over 90 days. A dollar near a one-year high makes gold more expensive outside the US and is a persistent headwind. The **10-year real yield** is **2.79%**, up 0.13 points over 30 days and 0.45 points over 90 days, and higher than **92%** of the past year's readings. Rising real yields lift the opportunity cost of holding an asset that pays no income. The nominal 10-year Treasury yield is **4.91%**, while the 10-year inflation breakeven has eased to **2.12%** — so the move up in yields is being driven by real rates, which is precisely the mix gold likes least.

## What is driving the market

Three dated developments explain the pressure:

- **A near-certain December Fed hike.** By 2026-11-20, markets were pricing roughly a 96-99% probability of a 25 basis-point hike at the 2026-12-09 FOMC meeting. Higher policy rates reinforce the dollar and real yields.
- **Rising real yields.** The 10-year real yield climbed from about 2.66% on 2026-11-09 to roughly 2.88% by 2026-11-18, a direct drag on gold.
- **Lower bank targets.** On 2026-11-05, Goldman Sachs cut its end-2026 gold target from $4,650 to $4,150, one of several reductions from once-lofty forecasts.

Gold also touched a 14-month low near $3,513.54 on 2026-11-20 and logged its worst week in eight months, so today's rebound comes after a steep decline rather than from a position of strength.

## Short-term outlook (1-4 weeks)

The short-term scorecard reads **-5**, a baseline **SELL**. The components are consistent: a strongly adverse 20-day return, price below the 50-day average, a rising real yield and a strongly adverse 30-day dollar move. The lone supportive factor is contrarian — the price has fallen far enough below its 50-day average that it is stretched to the downside — but it is outweighed. There is no dated, bullish event within the last 10 days to justify stepping the call up, so it stays at the default: **SELL, medium confidence**. The single daily bounce of 2.26% is already reflected in prices and does not change the measured setup.

**What would change this view:** a daily close **above $4,121** would break the short-term call.

## Long-term outlook (3-12 months)

The long-term scorecard reads **-6**, a baseline **SELL** with every factor adverse: price below both the 50-day and 200-day averages, a bearish 50-day-versus-200-day crossover, a deeply negative 90-day return, a large distance from the 52-week high, and rising real yields and dollar over 90 days. The cut to bank forecasts points the same way. With no dated bullish catalyst to offset this, the call holds at the default: **SELL, high confidence**.

**What would change this view:** a daily close **above $4,673** would break the long-term call.

## Risks to the view

The outlook is not one-directional. The clearest risk is the **2026-12-09 Fed decision**: a hike that is already fully priced, paired with softer guidance, could take pressure off real yields and the dollar and allow gold to firm. Because the dollar and real yields are both historically stretched — the dollar above every reading of the past year — any reversal in those drivers could be sharp, and gold's deep discount to its moving averages leaves room for a counter-trend bounce. A renewed geopolitical shock or an abrupt turn in risk sentiment could also lift safe-haven demand. For now, though, the measured factors dominate, and both horizons describe conditions that look more challenging than supportive for gold.
